extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and designers interested in architectural aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for producing architecture that expresses power and sublimity: how to choose aims (beauty vs. power), use size, form, masonry, light and shade, and placement to achieve a majestic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between beauty and sublimity (no compromise)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is well to determine at first whether the building is to be markedly beautiful, or markedly sublime; the choice must be a decided one, without compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming for sublimity, focus on largeness of scale and weight rather than timidly splitting resources across many decorative effects. Avoid attempting to be 'universally excellent' in small ways (painting, gilding, small steeples) if that prevents achieving the single deep effect required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two intellectual Lamps: gathering (veneration) and governing (dominion)
rubrics_metrics.description: All building shows man either as gathering (a just and humble veneration for the works of God) or governing (an understanding of dominion received by man); these are the two great intellectual Lamps of Architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs should consciously express one or the other: derive beauty from natural forms when following the 'gathering' lamp; express human arrangement and authority when following the 'governing' lamp. They may be harmonised, but their roles should be recognised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to express abstract power and sympathy with nature's sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture should have a sympathy with what is most sublime in natural things, and aim to express abstract power so that human works may receive added glory from association with nature's mightiest works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate forms, arrangements, or gestures that echo natural grandeur (cliffs, pinnacles, cones) so the building can stand in reverent relation to the landscape rather than merely imitating small natural details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use size/magnitude deliberately to achieve sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every increase of magnitude bestows upon a design a certain degree of nobleness; the architect should not be withheld from reaching largeness of scale if aiming for sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the building attains at least the minimal magnitude at which sublimity begins (an effect so large that a human figure appears small beside it). Place large masses where they are not opposed by larger natural features; site choice can make or break the perception of size (examples: Beauvais choir, St. Peter's placement errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate resources on a single deep effect rather than many small ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a crust about the impressible part of men's minds which must be pierced through; one deep thrust anywhere is better than many small superficial decorations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If choosing size as the means of impact, abandon decoration; a huge stone or mass will be worth far more than an army of pinnacles or tesselated pavements. Choose a clear point of attack and concentrate funds and design energy there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present the building so its extreme points are seen at once (continuous bounding line)
rubrics_metrics.description: A building, in order to show its magnitude, must be bounded as much as possible by continuous lines so that its extreme points can be seen all at once; one visible bounding line from top to bottom and from end to end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid violent breaks of the terminal bounding line (projecting cornices or recessed upper portions) which make the continuity and measurable length of that line unknowable. Where possible, design so the eye can take in the whole vertical extent (examples: cathedral towers detached as campaniles; Florence cathedral dome is felt from one point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place towers/height where their full height is visible (avoid placing over the cross)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the height of a tower is to be made apparent, it must be at the west end or detached as a campanile; towers over the cross lose their grandeur because the eye cannot trace the full vertical line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For maximum impact of height, consider detaching the tower or placing it where continuous vertical lines are visible; study Lombard and Lombard-Italian examples (campaniles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor true vertical bounding lines often with substantial projection
rubrics_metrics.description: The true vertical, or the vertical with a solemn frown of projection, gives a nobler character than mere projecting shelves; the whole wall must 'nod as well as frown.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design projections that are substantial (propped machicolations, grand swells) rather than small superficial cornices; examples praised include the Palazzo Vecchio and Tour de Beurre niches at Rouen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather mass into broad, square areas for maximum power
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings that seem the vastest are those gathered into a mighty square, where length, breadth, and height approach equality; breadth/area is a key element of sublime architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When power is the object, choose outlines approaching the square or large unbroken surfaces; the square and circle (and their solids cube/sphere) are elements of utmost power. Use broad surface to evoke horizon-like effects and allow play of light and storm to mark the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types: interest in walls (surface breadth) vs interest in lines (tracery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture divides into buildings whose interest is in their walls and those whose interest is in the lines dividing their walls; for abstract power and awfulness the principle of broad wall surface predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the principle appropriate to intent: wall-focused (broad unbroken surfaces) when aiming for power; line/tracery-focused (columns, frieze, tracery) when aiming for delicate beauty or grace. Material and stone quality can affect which principle works best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose forms appropriate to intent: square/cube/sphere for power, elongated series for grace
rubrics_metrics.description: The square and circle (with their relative solids) are the areas of power, while grace and perfect proportion require elongation in some direction; elongated forms can gain sublimity by continued series of marked features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use squares/cubes/spheres to express space and surface power; use arcades, aisles, and repeated mouldings to communicate magnitude in elongated buildings. The Doge's Palace is cited as a model combining both principles successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show masonry honestly and use appropriate masonry scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The masonry of a building is to be shown; the opposition of large stones to divided masonry gives a noble character. Smaller buildings require bolder masonry, and masonry should accommodate itself frankly to conditions and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conceal construction; use large stones, single-piece shafts, massy lintels where appropriate to express ability to handle vast masses. Avoid too-fine joints on columns or small stones that read as trellis (example: St. Madeleine facade problem). For buildings under majestic size, using massy stones can raise their nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect material in finish: match finish to stone character
rubrics_metrics.description: If building in marble or soft limestone, take advantage of its ease by making delicate designs and smooth chiselled surfaces; if building in granite or lava, it is often folly to polish—better to make the design granitic and leave blocks rudely squared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose finish and level of smoothing according to material; do not waste labor polishing granite when the same effort could raise scale. The natural cleavage and ruggedness of stone can convey brotherhood with mountain heart and real magnificence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide wall surfaces by masses of light and shade or by traced linear hues
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions of design are necessarily into masses of light and shade or else by traced hues (linear division); a wall surface is to an architect what a white canvas is to a painter, but the wall already has sublimity dangerous to break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat large wall surfaces carefully—decide whether to emphasize broad light-and-shadow masses (architectural) or linear incisions/projections that make traced hues (e.g., Henry VII's chapel panelling). Remember that architectural constraints make positive shade more vital than painterly subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make definite, positive shadow a chief means of sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive shade is a more necessary and more sublime thing in an architect's hands than in a painter's; after size and weight, the power of architecture depends on the quantity (space or intenseness) of its shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for definite, deep shadows (through projections, recesses, arcades) because architects cannot rely on tempering light with color as painters do. Prioritize shadow-creating elements to give the building human sympathy and the required darkness for majestic expression.
